docs.title: SWSDE Diabetes Data
docs.text: This site contains information about diabetes datasets and tools developed by the University of Exeter, NHS and NHS South West Secure Data Environment (SWSDE), including the Diabetes Core Dataset and Diabetes genomics database. It also contains information on related projects. More information on data available in the NHS SWSDE can be found on the HDR UK Health Data Research Gateway.

docs.title: Diabetes Core Dataset (DIA-Core)
docs.text:
The Diabetes Core Dataset (DIA-Core) defines a standardised set of variables describing diabetes diagnosis, classification, treatment, and key outcomes, derived from routinely collected health data. It is designed to support consistent, reproducible analyses across studies by providing clear variable definitions, reusable codelists, and explicit implementation rules for data extraction and derivation. This dataset was agreed by expert consensus with input from patients and the public. It was developed as part of a 2025-2026 NHS-funded driver project (press releases: 1 and 2). A preprint version of the manuscript describing the development and content of the Diabetes Core Dataset is available here.

The Diabetes Core Dataset is also listed as a tool on the HDR UK Health Data Research Gateway.

The DIA-Core specification and implementation framework includes the following resources:

  • Diabetes Core Dataset specification
  • Standardised input data requirements
  • Stage 1: Diabetes cohort ascertainment and classification
  • Stage 2: Derivation of the remaining core dataset variables

A follow-on HDRS-funded Technical Transformation project (October 2026–March 2027) aims to implement DIA-Core within the North East and North Cumbria (NENC) Secure Data Environment (SDE), building on the initial pilot implementation within the Kent, Medway and Sussex SDE. As part of this project, we are further developing the DIA-Core implementation framework, including standardised input data requirements, streamlined phenotyping algorithms, reusable codelists and technical documentation. The project aims to establish a validated, research-ready diabetes dataset within NENC using routinely collected primary care and linked hospital and ambulance data, whilst supporting consistent and scalable implementation of DIA-Core across the wider NHS SDE Network.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Identification of cardiovascular disease in routinely collected electronic health records (EHR), including ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, stroke, transient ischaemic attack, heart failure, hypertension and peripheral arterial disease.

We recommend deriving individual cardiovascular disease phenotypes separately to enable investigation of specific cardiovascular outcomes as well as composite outcomes.

For the ascertainment of acute cardiovascular events, we recommend using the phenotyping algorithms developed by the BHF Data Science Centre's SCORE-CVD project (Standardising Clinical Outcome measures in Routinely collected Electronic healthcare systems data). These algorithms were developed through expert consensus to standardise cardiovascular outcome ascertainment using routinely collected health data.

Primary care diagnostic codelists should also be used to capture recorded cardiovascular disease history, including events that predate the availability of linked hospital data.

docs.title: Acute MI events
docs.text:
We recommend using the SCORE-CVD myocardial infarction phenotyping algorithm to identify first and recurrent MI events using Hospital Episode Statistics Admitted Patient Care (HES APC) and Office for National Statistics (ONS) mortality data.

The algorithm uses ICD-10 codes I21 and I22, incorporating information on continuous inpatient spells, diagnosis position and timing of events to identify individual MI events and avoid double counting across data sources.

docs.text:
• SCORE-CVD MI phenotyping algorithm repository
  • R implementation and documentation
  • Databricks implementation
  • SCORE-CVD MI ICD-10 codelist

The R implementation also includes simulated data and automated tests to support implementation in new data environments.

docs.title: Recorded history of MI
docs.text:
Primary care diagnostic codes can provide additional information on recorded MI history.

  • Exeter MI SNOMED CT codelist

docs.title: DIA-Core implementation
docs.text:
Apply the SCORE-CVD MI algorithm to linked hospital and mortality records for individuals in the diabetes cohort, where these data are available.

Retain all identified MI events, including patient identifier, event date, event sequence (first or recurrent event) and source of ascertainment, where available.

Information on MI history derived from primary care diagnostic codes should be retained but distinguished from acute events identified using the SCORE-CVD algorithm.

docs.title: Acute stroke events
docs.text:
We recommend using the SCORE-CVD stroke phenotyping algorithm to identify first and recurrent stroke events using linked HES APC and ONS mortality data.

The algorithm distinguishes the following stroke subtypes:

Stroke subtype Default ICD-10 codes Ischaemic stroke I63 Haemorrhagic stroke I60, I61 Unknown stroke subtype I64

The algorithm incorporates information on continuous inpatient spells, diagnosis position, timing of events and mortality records. Configurable parameters allow adaptation to different research requirements.

Simulated data and validation scripts are also provided within the R implementation.

docs.title: Recorded history of stroke
docs.text:
Primary care diagnostic codes can provide additional information on recorded stroke history.

  • Exeter stroke SNOMED CT codelist

docs.title: DIA-Core implementation
docs.text:
Apply the SCORE-CVD stroke algorithm to linked hospital and mortality records for individuals in the diabetes cohort, where these data are available.

Retain all identified stroke events, including patient identifier, event date, stroke subtype, event sequence (first or recurrent event), fatal stroke status and source of ascertainment.

Algorithm parameters should be selected according to the intended research application and documented.

Information on stroke history derived from primary care diagnostic codes should be retained but distinguished from acute events identified using the SCORE-CVD algorithm.

docs.title: Heart failure
docs.text:
The BHF Data Science Centre has undertaken a heart failure phenotype benchmarking project to compare different approaches to identifying heart failure using routinely collected electronic health records.

The project provides codelists and implementation code for multiple heart failure phenotype definitions, incorporating evidence from primary care records, hospital admissions and medication records.

docs.title: Codelists and implementation resources
docs.text:
• Heart failure phenotype benchmarking repository
  • Heart failure phenotype codelists
  • Phenotype definitions and supporting documentation
  • Data curation and phenotype implementation code
  • Exeter heart failure SNOMED CT codelist

docs.title: DIA-Core implementation
docs.text:
Heart failure should be identified using primary care and linked secondary care records, where available.

We recommend distinguishing recorded heart failure diagnoses from hospital admissions for heart failure, retaining dates and sources of ascertainment to support both prevalent disease ascertainment and longitudinal outcome analyses.

The choice of heart failure phenotype definition should be informed by the findings of the benchmarking project, the available data sources and the intended research application. The selected definition and any local adaptations should be documented.

docs.title: Other cardiovascular disease phenotypes
docs.text: Additional cardiovascular disease phenotypes can be derived using primary care diagnostic codes and linked secondary care diagnostic and procedure codes.

docs.title: Codelists
docs.text:
The following SNOMED CT codelists are available from the University of Exeter CPRD codelist repository.

Phenotype SNOMED CT codelist Ischaemic heart disease Exeter IHD codelist Angina Exeter angina codelist Transient ischaemic attack Exeter TIA codelist Hypertension Exeter hypertension codelist Peripheral arterial disease Exeter PAD codelist Revascularisation Exeter revascularisation codelist

Additional codelists are available from the HDR UK Phenotype Library and OpenCodelists.

docs.title: General implementation rules
docs.text:
• Check that event dates are consistent with data source coverage and patient dates of birth and death.
  • Retain longitudinal information on cardiovascular events and diagnoses.
  • Distinguish historical diagnostic records from acute events where possible.
  • Avoid double counting events recorded across multiple data sources.
  • Retain individual cardiovascular disease phenotypes to enable derivation of composite outcomes according to specific research requirements.
  • Document the source, version and configuration of each codelist and phenotyping algorithm used.
  • Document any limitations arising from unavailable or incomplete linked data.

See the standardised DIA-Core input data requirements for further information on the data required to implement these phenotypes.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Identification and staging of chronic kidney disease (CKD) using routinely collected electronic health records (EHR), including information on kidney function, albuminuria, CKD diagnoses, dialysis and kidney transplantation.

We recommend following the CKD phenotyping algorithm developed by the BHF Data Science Centre's Kidney Data Science Catalyst.

docs.title: CKD phenotyping algorithm
docs.text:
The Kidney Data Science Catalyst algorithm combines evidence from primary care records, linked secondary care records and demographic information to identify and stage CKD.

The algorithm incorporates:

  • Primary care SNOMED CT codes for CKD diagnoses and kidney-related procedures.
  • Secondary care ICD-10 diagnostic codes.
  • Secondary care OPCS-4 procedure codes.
  • Serum creatinine measurements used to derive estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
  • Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) measurements.
  • Evidence of chronicity from repeated measurements.
  • Evidence of dialysis and kidney transplantation.

The algorithm derives eGFR using the CKD-EPI 2021 equation and incorporates CKD staging based on kidney function (G stage) and albuminuria (A stage).

The algorithm also includes rules for assigning CKD status where laboratory measurements or other information are incomplete.

Additional information on approaches previously used to derive longitudinal CKD stages in CPRD is available from the University of Exeter CPRD codelist repository.

docs.title: DIA-Core implementation
docs.text:
Apply the Kidney Data Science Catalyst CKD phenotyping algorithm to available primary care and linked secondary care data for individuals in the diabetes cohort.

The following information should be retained to support downstream research:

  • CKD status and estimated date of diagnosis.
  • CKD stage based on kidney function (G stage).
  • Albuminuria stage (A stage).
  • Recorded dialysis history.
  • Recorded kidney transplantation history.
  • Longitudinal serum creatinine and eGFR measurements.
  • Longitudinal urine ACR measurements.
  • Source of evidence used to identify and stage CKD.

Where possible, retain dates of changes in CKD stage and dates of kidney-related procedures to enable research into longitudinal CKD progression.

Where the upstream algorithm provides a single CKD status or stage, additional longitudinal processing may be required to derive changes in CKD stage over time.

docs.title: General implementation rules
docs.text:
• Check that clinical event and measurement dates are consistent with patient dates of birth and death and data source coverage.
  • Standardise serum creatinine and ACR measurement units.
  • Apply the recommended rules for confirming chronicity and assigning CKD stage.
  • Document the eGFR equation and algorithm version used.
  • Document any differences between the recommended algorithm and local implementation, including differences in laboratory measurement availability.
  • Where secondary care data are unavailable, document the limitations of CKD ascertainment using primary care data alone.

See the standardised DIA-Core input data requirements for further information on the data required to implement this phenotype.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Defining diabetes in EHR data. We recommend using codelists from the Defining Diabetes HDR UK Diabetes Data Science Catalyst (DDSC) project (codelist also available at the HDR UK Phenotype Library here) which categorise diabetes codes by diabetes type (type 1, type 2, NOS [not otherwise specified], other). Alternative codelists can be found on the HDR UK Phenotype Library and OpenCodelists.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Check to make sure the date is within the range expected given the data source and patient DOB and death dates.

  • We recommend following the Defining Diabetes HDR UK Diabetes Data Science Catalyst (DDSC) algorithms to define diabetes cases, diabetes diagnosis dates and diabetes type. An overview of the algorithms are available via the HDR UK Phenotype library here and detailed information on derivation and validation are available here. These algorithms are used in the step-by-step instructions for diabetes cohort ascertainment and classification.

  • Diabetes cases: (1) a diabetes diagnostic code (in primary or secondary care), (2) at least six months of insulin prescription data (see diabetes medications), or (3) two consecutive elevated (>=48 mmol/mol) HbA1c measurements (see HbA1c).

  • Diabetes diagnosis dates: the earliest of (1) the first recorded diabetes code of any type, or (2) the first elevated (>=48 mmol/mol) HbA1c result from a qualifying pair (two results within two years), but only if this HbA1c occurred more than one year before the first diagnosis code. Using this method, diagnosis date cannot be calculated for diabetes cases with at least 6 months of insulin data who have no diabetes codes or elevated HbA1cs. We recommend removing diagnosis dates within -30 to +90 days (inclusive) of GP registration start date as they may represent pre-existing diagnoses (similar to https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/10/e017989 except we also excluded diagnoses up to 30 days before registration as our analysis in CPRD showed an excess of diagnoses in this period). We also recommend removing diagnosis dates where insulin initiation was more than a year prior to diagnosis. It may not be possible to determine diagnosis dates in some datasets if historical data is not available. Accuracy can be improved by a) ignoring codes within the year of birth for those with type 2 diabetes, and/or b) ignoring diabetes codes which clearly do not relate to diagnosis e.g. in CPRD ignore diabetes codes with obstype=4 as these represent family history.

  • Classifying type 1 and type 2 diabetes in those with codes for both: if not currently on insulin (no prescriptions in last 6 months) and >1 year between diagnosis and earliest insulin script, categorise as type 2. If either currently on insulin or started insulin within 1 year of diagnosis, use the ratio of type 1:type 2 codes to assign type. The DDSC algorithm evaluated three approaches to assigning type 1 based on type 1:type 2 code ratios: V2.0 (Majority rule): Type 1 codes > Type 2 codes; V2.1 (Klompas): Type 1 codes > 0.5 × Type 2 codes; V2.2 (Exeter rule): Type 1 codes ≥ 2 × Type 2 codes. V2.0 demonstrates the best balance of specificity and sensitivity for type 1 diabetes classification based on genetic validation; V2.1 and V2.2 have greater specificity but with reduced sensitivity.

  • Further work needs to be carried out to classify other diabetes types within the 'Diabetes Other' classification resulting from the algorithm, e.g. we have previously ascertained type 3c cases by requiring a record of a pancreatic condition (acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, or haemochromatosis) prior to a diagnosis of diabetes.

docs.title: Diabetes remission and resolution
docs.text:
Diabetes remission should be recorded separately from the underlying diabetes type. Diabetes resolved codes are distinct from remission codes and may be used where a previous diabetes diagnosis was incorrect.

The following SNOMED CT codes are included in the DDSC diabetes diagnostic codelists:

SNOMED CT code Description Event category Diabetes type associated with code 703136005 Diabetes mellitus in remission Remission Unspecified 703137001 Type I diabetes mellitus in remission Remission Type 1 703138006 Type II diabetes mellitus in remission Remission Type 2 315051004 Diabetes resolved Resolved Unspecified

Sources: DDSC type 1 diabetes codelist, DDSC type 2 diabetes codelist and DDSC diabetes NOS codelist.

Identify these codes explicitly rather than filtering on the DDSC Remission label, which does not consistently distinguish remission from resolution or identify type-specific remission codes.

docs.title: DIA-Core implementation
docs.text:
Retain all recorded remission and resolution events in a longitudinal table:

Variable Description patient_id Pseudonymous patient identifier event_date Date of recorded remission or resolution clinical_code Original SNOMED CT code event_category Remission or resolved code_diabetes_type Diabetes type associated with the code (type 1, type 2 or unspecified)

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Retain remission and resolution codes as separate event categories, including all recorded instances and dates.
  • Preserve the underlying diabetes type and diagnosis date derived through the diabetes cohort ascertainment algorithm.
  • Do not use a historical remission code alone to infer current remission status.
  • Do not automatically exclude individuals from the diabetes cohort solely because a diabetes resolved code is recorded.
  • The initial DIA-Core implementation captures recorded remission. Deriving remission from longitudinal HbA1c and glucose-lowering medication history, including the end of remission, is outside the scope of this initial implementation.

For CPRD-specific implementations, an Exeter remission and resolution medcode codelist is also available; the SNOMED CT codes above are recommended for DIA-Core.

docs.title: Foot complications and lower limb amputation
Description
docs.text:
Identification of diabetes-related foot complications using routinely collected electronic health records (EHR), including primary care clinical codes and linked secondary care diagnostic and procedure codes.

The Diabetes Core Dataset includes:

  • Foot ulceration.
  • Foot infection.
  • Loss of sensation.
  • Loss of foot pulses.
  • Lower limb amputation (minor and major).

docs.title: Foot ulceration, infection and ischaemia
docs.text: The University of Exeter has developed a combined codelist for foot ulceration, infection and ischaemia.

docs.title: Primary care
docs.text:
• Exeter foot ulcer, infection and ischaemia CPRD medcode codelist

A corresponding SNOMED CT codelist has been developed and is pending inclusion in the public codelist repository.

docs.title: Secondary care
docs.text:
• Exeter foot ulcer, infection and ischaemia ICD-10 codelist

The current ICD-10 codelist identifies lower limb ulceration.

docs.title: Foot screening and risk assessment
docs.text:
Information on foot complications and risk can also be obtained from clinical codes used in the NHS Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF).

Historical QOF foot assessment codes (2004–2010) capture individual examination findings, including:

  • Presence or absence of foot pulses.
  • Normal or abnormal vibration sense.
  • Normal or abnormal 10g monofilament sensation.

From 2011 onwards, QOF codes also capture overall foot risk classifications:

  • Low risk.
  • Moderate risk.
  • High risk.
  • Ulcerated foot.

The University of Exeter, working with collaborators at the University of Bristol, has incorporated these codes into a CPRD foot screening codelist.

  • Foot screening CPRD medcode codelist

SNOMED CT equivalents and further implementation guidance for combining historical examination findings are pending.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
• Abnormal vibration sense and abnormal monofilament sensation provide evidence of loss of sensation.
  • Absent foot pulses provide evidence of loss of pulse.
  • Ulcerated foot assessment codes provide additional evidence of foot ulceration.
  • Moderate and high risk classifications may reflect sensory loss, impaired circulation or both, and should not be used in isolation to infer loss of sensation or absent pulses.
  • Retain overall foot risk classifications as supplementary information where available.
  • Retain laterality (left or right foot) where recorded.

docs.title: Charcot foot
docs.text:
Charcot foot can be identified as an additional diabetes-related foot complication using the following codelists:

  • Exeter Charcot foot SNOMED CT codelist
  • Exeter Charcot foot ICD-10 codelist

docs.title: Lower limb amputation
docs.text: Lower limb amputations should be identified primarily using secondary care procedure records, supplemented by primary care records where available.

docs.title: Primary care
docs.text: • Exeter lower limb amputation CPRD medcode codelist

docs.title: Secondary care
docs.text:
• Exeter lower limb amputation OPCS-4 codelist

The codelist includes the following OPCS-4 code groups:

Code Description X09 Amputation of leg X10 Amputation of foot X11 Amputation of toe

Major and minor amputations should be distinguished using procedure-level information. Further guidance on classification and primary care SNOMED CT codelists is pending.

docs.title: DIA-Core implementation
docs.text:
We recommend retaining longitudinal information on each of the following components separately, where available:

Component Data sources Foot ulceration Primary and secondary care clinical codes Foot infection Primary and secondary care clinical codes Loss of sensation Primary care foot examination codes Absent foot pulses Primary care foot examination codes Lower limb amputation Primary care clinical codes and secondary care OPCS-4 procedure codes

Supplementary information may include foot ischaemia, foot risk classification, normal examination findings and Charcot foot.

For each record, retain the patient identifier, event date, original clinical code, derived phenotype, data source and laterality where available.

Where a codelist combines several complications, retain the original clinical code to support subsequent refinement of the phenotype.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Check that clinical event dates are consistent with data source coverage and patient dates of birth and death.
  • Retain all recorded foot complications, examination findings and amputation procedures.
  • Distinguish normal and abnormal examination findings.
  • Distinguish foot risk assessments from established foot complications.
  • Distinguish recorded disease or amputation history from newly recorded events and procedures where possible.
  • Distinguish major and minor amputations where coding allows.
  • Remove trailing hash (#) characters from SNOMED CT code identifiers before use and remove duplicate codes within each codelist.
  • Document the codelist versions and phenotype definitions used.

docs.title: Quality assurance
docs.text:
• Number and percentage of patients with each foot complication.
  • Number and percentage of patients with recorded foot examination findings.
  • Distribution of normal and abnormal examination findings.
  • Distribution of foot risk classifications where available.
  • Number of patients with major and minor amputations.
  • Frequency of individual clinical codes.
  • Distribution of event dates.
  • Contribution of primary and secondary care data to each phenotype.

docs.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
Description
docs.text:
Identification of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) using routinely collected electronic health records (EHR).

These acute complications can be identified using primary care clinical codes and linked secondary care diagnostic codes, with hospital admission data providing an important source of information on acute episodes.

docs.title: Primary care (SNOMED CT)
docs.text:
• Exeter hyperglycaemic crisis SNOMED CT codelist

The codelist includes codes for DKA, HHS and other or unspecified hyperglycaemic crises.

Remove trailing hash (#) characters from SNOMED CT code identifiers before use and remove duplicate codes.

DKA and HHS can be distinguished using the individual clinical codes. Codes that do not specifically identify either DKA or HHS should be retained separately rather than assigned to either category.

docs.title: Secondary care (ICD-10)
docs.text:
• Exeter DKA ICD-10 codelist

The codelist includes diabetes with ketoacidosis codes across different diabetes types.

A separate ICD-10 codelist for HHS is not currently available in the Exeter codelist repository. Diabetes with coma codes should not automatically be interpreted as HHS, as these may also capture other acute metabolic complications.

docs.title: DIA-Core implementation
docs.text:
We recommend retaining longitudinal information on DKA and HHS separately where coding allows.

Component Data sources Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) Primary care SNOMED CT and secondary care ICD-10 codes Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) Primary care SNOMED CT codes, supplemented by secondary care information where available Other or unspecified hyperglycaemic crisis Primary and secondary care clinical codes where appropriate Hospitalisation with DKA or HHS Secondary care admission and diagnostic records

For each record, retain the patient identifier, event date, original clinical code, derived phenotype and data source.

For hospital admissions, retain admission and discharge dates, hospital spell identifiers where available, and diagnostic code position. This allows hospitalisations primarily due to DKA or HHS to be distinguished from admissions where these conditions are recorded as secondary diagnoses.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Check that clinical event dates are consistent with data source coverage and patient dates of birth and death.
  • Retain all recorded DKA and HHS clinical codes.
  • Distinguish DKA and HHS where coding allows.
  • Retain codes with uncertain or unspecified subtype separately.
  • Distinguish primary care records of previous events from newly occurring acute episodes where possible.
  • Distinguish primary and secondary hospital diagnoses.
  • Avoid counting multiple diagnostic records within the same continuous hospital stay as separate acute episodes.
  • Document the codelist versions and phenotype definitions used.

docs.title: Quality assurance
docs.text:
• Number and percentage of patients with recorded DKA and HHS.
  • Number of hospitalisations with DKA and HHS.
  • Frequency of individual clinical codes.
  • Distribution of event dates.
  • Distribution of events by diabetes type.
  • Contribution of primary and secondary care data to each phenotype.
  • Distribution of primary and secondary hospital diagnostic positions.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Identification of diabetic retinopathy using routinely collected electronic health records (EHR), including primary care clinical codes and linked secondary care diagnostic and procedure codes.

The University of Exeter retinopathy codelists were updated in 2025 to distinguish severe and non-severe retinopathy. Additional codelists are available for complications associated with severe retinopathy, including vitreous and pre-retinal haemorrhage and blindness and visual impairment.

docs.title: Primary care (SNOMED CT)
docs.text:
Phenotype Codelist Non-severe retinopathy Exeter non-severe retinopathy SNOMED CT codelist Severe retinopathy Exeter severe retinopathy SNOMED CT codelist Vitreous and pre-retinal haemorrhage Exeter vitreous haemorrhage SNOMED CT codelist Blindness and visual impairment Exeter blindness and visual impairment SNOMED CT codelist

Remove trailing hash (#) characters from SNOMED CT code identifiers before use and remove duplicate codes within each codelist.

docs.title: Secondary care (ICD-10)
docs.text: Phenotype Codelist Non-severe retinopathy Exeter non-severe retinopathy ICD-10 codelist Severe retinopathy Exeter severe retinopathy ICD-10 codelist Vitreous and pre-retinal haemorrhage Exeter vitreous haemorrhage ICD-10 codelist Blindness and visual impairment Exeter blindness and visual impairment ICD-10 codelist

docs.title: Secondary care (OPCS-4)
docs.text:
• Exeter severe retinopathy OPCS-4 codelist

The OPCS-4 codelist includes retinal photocoagulation and intravitreal injection procedures.

docs.title: Retinopathy severity
docs.text: The existing Exeter codelists distinguish severe and non-severe retinopathy. The severe retinopathy codelists include proliferative retinopathy, more advanced forms of non-proliferative retinopathy and evidence of retinal treatment.

docs.title: Composite severe retinopathy
docs.text:
An existing Exeter approach to defining composite severe retinopathy in CPRD Aurum and linked hospital data combines evidence of:

  • Severe retinopathy, including retinal photocoagulation.
  • Vitreous and pre-retinal haemorrhage.
  • Blindness and visual impairment.

The date of composite severe retinopathy is defined as the earliest recorded date of any of these components.

A more specific alternative definition requires previous evidence of retinopathy for blindness or visual impairment to contribute to the composite outcome.

docs.title: DIA-Core implementation
docs.text:
We recommend retaining longitudinal information on each of the following components separately:

Component Data sources Non-severe retinopathy Primary and secondary care diagnostic codes Severe retinopathy Primary and secondary care diagnostic and procedure codes Vitreous and pre-retinal haemorrhage Primary and secondary care diagnostic codes Blindness and visual impairment Primary and secondary care clinical codes Retinal treatment procedures Primary care procedure codes and secondary care OPCS-4 codes

For each record, retain the patient identifier, event date, original clinical code, derived phenotype and data source.

Retaining individual components allows researchers to derive alternative definitions of retinopathy severity and composite outcomes without repeating the initial data extraction.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Check that clinical event dates are consistent with data source coverage and patient dates of birth and death.
  • Retain all recorded retinopathy diagnoses and relevant procedures.
  • Retain separate dates for the earliest evidence of each phenotype.
  • Distinguish recorded disease history from treatment procedures and newly recorded diagnoses where possible.
  • Do not assume that severe and non-severe retinopathy are mutually exclusive.
  • Document any additional criteria used to establish that diagnoses and procedures are attributable to diabetic retinopathy.
  • Document the codelist versions and phenotype definitions used.

docs.title: Quality assurance
docs.text:
• Number and percentage of patients with each retinopathy phenotype.
  • Number of patients with evidence of both severe and non-severe retinopathy.
  • Frequency of individual clinical codes.
  • Distribution of event dates and age at first recorded event.
  • Contribution of primary and secondary care data to each phenotype.
  • Contribution of individual components to any composite severe retinopathy outcome.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Identifying and cleaning measured urine ACR (albumin-creatinine ratio) values in EHR data. Three codelists are provided: urine ACR, urine albumin and urine creatinine.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Values associated with ACR codes should be used preferentially, and separate albumin and creatinine values used to calculate ACR where these are not available.

To note: steps 1-3 below should be carried out in this order to produce a standardised end result:

  1. Standardise measured ACR values to mg/mmol using recorded unit information where available. Where ACR is calculated from separate urine albumin and creatinine measurements, ensure that the component measurements are expressed in compatible units.
  2. Remove ACR values less than 0 and greater than 450 mg/mmol as these are considered implausible.

  3. If multiple ACR values are recorded on the same day for a patient, take the mean.

  4. Check to make sure the date is within the range expected given the data source and patient DOB and death dates.

docs.title: Origins
docs.text: • The origins of the SNOMED codelists were the Pathology Bounded Code List (PBCL).

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• Urine albumin-creatinine ratio SNOMED
  • Urine albumin SNOMED
  • Urine creatinine SNOMED

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Identifying and cleaning ALT (Alanine aminotransferase) values in EHR data.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
To note: steps 1-3 below should be carried out in this order to produce a standardised end result:

  1. Standardise values to U/L using recorded unit information where available.
  2. Remove values less than 0 and greater than 200 U/L as these are considered implausible.

  3. If multiple values are recorded on the same day for a patient, take the mean.

  4. Check to make sure the date is within the range expected given the data source and patient DOB and death dates.

docs.title: Origins
docs.text: • The origin of the SNOMED codelist was the Pathology Bounded Code List (PBCL).

docs.title: Data
docs.text: • ALT SNOMED

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Identifying and cleaning BMI values in EHR data. We recommend using the BMI marker codelist developed by the BHF HDR UK Diabetes Data Science Catalyst (DDSC) Defining Diabetes project.

docs.title: Codelists
docs.text:
• DDSC BMI markers SNOMED CT codelist

The codelist includes both BMI measurement concepts and categorical BMI findings. To derive continuous BMI, use recorded numerical measurement values; do not infer a numerical BMI from the category or range in a clinical code description alone.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
The plausibility thresholds below are intended for adult populations (aged 18 years and over). For children and adolescents, age-appropriate and, where relevant, sex-specific plausibility thresholds should be applied.

To note: steps 1-3 below should be carried out in this order to produce a standardised end result:

  1. Standardise values to kg/m² using recorded unit information where available.
  2. Remove values less than 15 and greater than 100 kg per square metre as these are implausible for adults.

  3. If multiple values are recorded on the same day for a patient, take the mean.

  4. Check to make sure the date is within the range expected given the data source and patient DOB and death dates.

docs.text: Identifying and cleaning systolic and diastolic blood pressure values in EHR data. We recommend using the SNOMED CT codelists developed by the University of Exeter.

docs.title: Codelists
docs.text:
• Exeter systolic blood pressure SNOMED CT codelist
  • Exeter diastolic blood pressure SNOMED CT codelist

Extract the snomedcode field, remove trailing hash (#) characters from code identifiers and remove duplicate codes before use. The codelists include measurement concepts and other clinical findings. Use associated numerical measurement values to derive continuous blood pressure; do not infer numerical values from clinical code descriptions alone. Retain measurement context (e.g. home, ambulatory or clinic readings) where available.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
To note: steps 1-3 below should be carried out in this order to produce a standardised end result:

  1. Standardise values to mmHg using recorded unit information where available.
  2. Systolic blood pressure (SBP): remove values less than 40 and greater than 270 mmHg as these are implausible. Diastolic blood pressure (DBP): remove values less than 20 and greater than 200 mmHg as these are implausible.

  3. If multiple values are recorded on the same day for a patient, take the mean (SBP and DBP processed separately).

  4. Check to make sure the date is within the range expected given the data source and patient DOB and death dates.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:

  4. Check to make sure the date is within the range expected given the data source and patient DOB and death dates.

docs.text: Defining alcohol consumption status using routinely collected electronic health records (EHR).

docs.title: Codelists
docs.text:
We recommend using the categorised SNOMED CT codelist developed by the University of Exeter:

  • Exeter alcohol SNOMED CT codelist

The codelist includes a category field distinguishing the following alcohol consumption levels:

Codelist category Alcohol consumption level AlcoholConsumptionLevel0 None AlcoholConsumptionLevel1 Within limits AlcoholConsumptionLevel2 Excess AlcoholConsumptionLevel3 Harmful

When using this codelist with SNOMED CT-coded data, extract the snomedcode and category fields, remove trailing hash (#) characters from code identifiers and remove duplicate code-category combinations. Check for codes assigned to multiple categories before implementation.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Check that observation dates are consistent with data source coverage and patient dates of birth and death.
  • Retain all recorded alcohol consumption categories and observation dates.
  • When deriving alcohol consumption status at a particular date, use the most recently recorded information on or before that date.
  • If a patient has previously been recorded with a level 3 code, categorise as level 3, reflecting a history of harmful alcohol consumption.
  • If multiple levels are recorded on the most recent date, take the highest level.
  • Individuals without recorded alcohol consumption information should be classified as missing or unknown.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This is a description of how date of birth can be defined when either date or date and month of birth are not provided.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Earliest possible date of birth is defined as the 1st of the month (where month of birth and year of birth available) / 1st January where only year of birth available
  • Patient date of birth is defined as the earliest of:
  • 15th of month of birth (where month of birth and year of birth available) / 1st July where only year of birth available
  • Earliest recorded code in records (excluding those before earliest possible date of birth)
  • Registration start date, where available (excluding before earliest possible date of birth)

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Defining ethnicity using routinely collected electronic health records (EHR), including primary care and linked secondary care records.

docs.title: Primary care
docs.text:
We recommend using the categorised SNOMED CT ethnicity codelist developed by OpenSAFELY:

  • OpenSAFELY ethnicity SNOMED CT codelist
  • Download codelist (CSV)

We recommend retaining the 16-level ethnicity classification provided in the Grouping_16 field of the codelist, from which broader ethnicity categories can be derived.

Further information on the completeness and consistency of ethnicity recording in primary care is available in the OpenSAFELY ethnicity study.

docs.title: Secondary care
docs.text:
Ethnicity recorded in linked secondary care data should be used to supplement primary care ethnicity where missing.

Hospital ethnicity codes should be mapped to the equivalent ethnicity categories used for primary care records, retaining the original codes and data source.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Primary care ethnicity should be used preferentially and supplemented with ethnicity recorded in linked secondary care data where missing. This approach is supported by Mathur et al. (2014), who demonstrated greater consistency of ethnicity recording in primary care than in Hospital Episode Statistics (HES).
  • Retain all recorded ethnicity codes and their observation dates where available.
  • Map primary care ethnicity codes to the 16-level classification using the Grouping_16 field of the OpenSAFELY codelist.
  • Map secondary care ethnicity codes to an equivalent classification before combining information across data sources.
  • Where multiple valid ethnicity codes are recorded, retain sufficient information to identify both the most frequently and most recently recorded ethnicity within each data source.
  • Missing, unknown and not stated ethnicity should be distinguished where possible.
  • Document the codelist version, ethnicity grouping and rules used to combine information from different data sources.

docs.title: Recommended default classification
docs.text:
For a single patient-level ethnicity variable, we recommend adapting the Exeter CPRD ethnicity algorithm to the 16-category classification:

  1. Within each data source, exclude missing, unknown and not stated categories from the classification counts. Include valid ethnicity categories even where the observation date is unavailable.
  2. Assign the most frequently recorded valid ethnicity category.
  3. If multiple categories are equally frequent, select the category with the most recent dated recording among the tied categories.
  4. If the tie cannot be resolved using available dates, including where conflicting tied categories occur on the same most recent date, assign unknown.
  5. Derive ethnicity separately in primary and secondary care. Use the primary care classification preferentially, supplementing with the secondary care classification if primary care ethnicity is missing or unknown.
  6. Derive broader ethnicity groupings from the assigned 16-category classification to ensure consistency between grouping levels.

Retain the source-specific counts and recency variables to support alternative classifications. The default is adapted from the Exeter approach rather than a requirement to reproduce its separate five-category and QRISK2 algorithms. Alternative frequency- and recency-based approaches have been evaluated by Shiekh et al. (2025).

docs.title: Recommended derived variables
docs.text:
For each patient, we recommend deriving:

Variable Description Ethnicity code counts Number of recorded ethnicity codes within each of the 16 ethnicity categories Most recent ethnicity Ethnicity category of the most recently recorded valid ethnicity code Most recent ethnicity date Date of the most recently recorded valid ethnicity code Most frequent ethnicity Most frequently recorded valid ethnicity category Assigned ethnicity Recommended 16-category ethnicity derived using the default classification above Ethnicity data source Source of the derived ethnicity information

Where ethnicity is available from both primary and secondary care, these variables should be derived separately for each data source.

Retaining both the frequency and recency of ethnicity recording enables assessment of consistency and supports alternative approaches to ethnicity ascertainment in downstream research.

Where possible, retain the original longitudinal ethnicity records alongside these derived variables.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Mathur et al. (2014). Completeness and usability of ethnicity data in UK-based primary care and hospital databases. Journal of Public Health.
  • Andrews et al. (2024). Consistency, completeness and external validity of ethnicity recording in NHS primary care records: a cohort study in 25 million patients' records at source using OpenSAFELY. BMC Medicine.
  • Shiekh SI, Williams R, Axson EL (2025). Development of an algorithm for ethnicity recording in cohorts from the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink primary care and linked Hospital Episode Statistics databases. BMJ Open.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Defining smoking status using routinely collected electronic health records (EHR).

docs.title: Codelists
docs.text:
We recommend using the categorised SNOMED CT codelist developed by the University of Exeter:

  • Exeter smoking SNOMED CT codelist

The codelist includes a category field describing smoking status.

When using this codelist with SNOMED CT-coded data, extract the snomedcode and category fields, remove trailing hash (#) characters from code identifiers and remove duplicate code-category combinations. Check for codes assigned to multiple categories before implementation.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Check that observation dates are consistent with data source coverage and patient dates of birth and death.
  • We recommend using three main smoking categories: non-smoker, ex-smoker and active smoker.
  • Active smokers may be further subdivided according to smoking intensity (e.g. cigarettes per day), where this information is available.
  • Retain all recorded smoking status categories and observation dates.
  • When deriving smoking status at a particular date, use the most recently recorded information on or before that date.
  • If non-smoker and ex-smoker are recorded on the same date, categorise that date as ex-smoker.
  • If active smoker is recorded on the same date as non-smoker or ex-smoker, look at the next most recent date. Repeat until a date with an unambiguous category is found.
  • If no unambiguous dated recording is available, assign unknown.
  • If the selected status is non-smoker but the individual has previously been recorded as an active smoker before the selected date, categorise as ex-smoker.
  • Individuals without recorded smoking status should be classified as missing or unknown.

These rules are based on the Exeter CPRD smoking algorithm. Assigning unknown where no unambiguous date is available is an explicit fallback for DIA-Core.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Diabetes Core Dataset (DIA-Core) defines a standardised set of variables describing diabetes diagnosis, classification, treatment and key outcomes, derived from routinely collected health data.

The dataset was agreed by expert consensus with input from patients and the public. Further information on the development and content of DIA-Core is available in the preprint manuscript.

The Diabetes Core Dataset is also listed as a tool on the HDR UK Health Data Research Gateway.

docs.title: Implementing the Diabetes Core Dataset
docs.text:
The DIA-Core implementation framework is designed to support consistent and reproducible implementation across Secure Data Environments (SDEs) and other routinely collected health data sources.

The DIA-Core implementation framework is under active development as part of the HDRS Technical Transformation project. Guidance is provided for all 30 core dataset variables, although some codelists and phenotype definitions require further refinement. Implementation and evaluation within the North East and North Cumbria SDE will inform subsequent updates.

Implementation involves two main stages:

docs.title: Stage 1: Diabetes cohort ascertainment and classification
docs.text:
Identification of individuals with diabetes, estimation of diabetes diagnosis date and age at diagnosis, and classification of diabetes type using algorithms developed by the BHF HDR UK Diabetes Data Science Catalyst (DDSC).

View Stage 1 implementation guidance.

docs.title: Stage 2: Derivation of the remaining core dataset variables
docs.text:
Extraction, cleaning and derivation of demographic information, clinical measurements, biomarkers, diabetes complications, lifestyle information and medication prescriptions.

View Stage 2 implementation guidance.

docs.title: Implementation pathway
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Local SDE data] --> B[Map to standardised input data requirements]
    B --> C[Stage 1: Diabetes cohort ascertainment and classification]
    C --> D[Stage 2: Derivation of remaining core variables]
    D --> E[Diabetes Core Dataset]
    F[Standardised codelists and phenotyping algorithms] --> C
    F --> D
    E --> G[Research and analysis]

A standardised input data specification defines the logical tables, variables and coding systems required to implement DIA-Core. This enables SDEs to map their local data structures to a common framework, identify gaps in data availability and facilitate consistent implementation across the NHS SDE Network.

Quality assurance checks are provided throughout the implementation guidance.

docs.title: Dataset structure
docs.text:
For each core variable, we recommend retaining all available instances for each patient, where applicable. This longitudinal structure, including repeated clinical measurements, medication prescriptions and clinical events, maximises flexibility for downstream research use.

All tables should be linkable using a consistent pseudonymous patient identifier.

The physical structure of the dataset may vary between SDEs, but variable definitions, coding systems and derivation rules should be consistent wherever possible.

docs.title: Stage 2: Derivation of the remaining DIA-Core variables
Overview
docs.text:
Following Stage 1: Diabetes cohort ascertainment and classification, the second stage of implementing the Diabetes Core Dataset (DIA-Core) involves deriving the remaining core dataset variables for individuals with diabetes.

We recommend retaining all available instances of each variable, where applicable, to maximise flexibility for downstream research. For example, the dataset should retain all cleaned BMI measurements, medication prescriptions and cardiovascular disease events, rather than only the most recent record.

See the standardised input data requirements for further information on the input tables, variables and coding systems required.

docs.title: 1. Demographics
docs.text:
Variable Codelists and implementation guidance Date of birth Date of birth Sex Recorded sex from patient demographics Ethnicity Ethnicity Date of death Preferentially derived from national mortality registration data where available

Output: one row per patient containing demographic information.

Quality assurance: distribution of age, sex and ethnicity, including missingness, and number of recorded deaths.

docs.title: 2. Diabetes features
docs.text:
Date and age at diabetes diagnosis and diabetes type are derived as part of Stage 1.

Information on diabetes remission should also be retained, where available, following the diabetes phenotype guidance.

docs.title: General principles for cleaning clinical measurements and biomarkers
docs.text:
• Standardise measurement units before applying plausibility thresholds.
  • Where recorded units are unavailable, use codelist-specific unit information or documented, measurement-specific rules to infer units where possible.
  • Measurements with units that cannot be reliably established should be flagged and excluded from cleaned measurement values where appropriate.
  • Apply age-appropriate plausibility thresholds, particularly when processing data from children and adolescents.
  • Retain original measurement values, units and clinical codes where possible to support quality assurance and reproducibility.
  • Document unit conversions, assumptions and any adaptations to the recommended cleaning rules.

Where available, primary care records should be supplemented with linked secondary care and mortality data. Recorded disease history should be distinguished from acute clinical events where possible.

We recommend building on existing phenotyping resources developed by the BHF Data Science Centre, including:

  • SCORE-CVD algorithms for identifying acute myocardial infarction and stroke events.
  • Heart Failure Phenotype Benchmarking resources for identifying heart failure.
  • Kidney Data Science Catalyst algorithm for identifying and staging chronic kidney disease.

Further information, including codelists, implementation code and guidance on applying these algorithms within DIA-Core, is provided on the cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease pages.

docs.title: Quality assurance
docs.text:
For continuous variables and dates, we recommend reporting the minimum, 25th percentile, median, 75th percentile, maximum and mode, where appropriate.

For categorical variables, we recommend reporting counts, percentages and missingness.

Data availability and completeness should be assessed for each core dataset variable, with any limitations in data coverage or adaptations to the recommended implementation documented.

docs.title: Final dataset
docs.text:
The final Diabetes Core Dataset comprises:

  • A patient-level diabetes cohort containing demographics and diabetes features.
  • Longitudinal clinical measurement and biomarker tables.
  • Longitudinal diabetes complication tables.
  • Longitudinal lifestyle information.
  • Longitudinal medication and device prescription tables.

All tables should be linkable using a consistent pseudonymous patient identifier.

The physical structure of the dataset may vary between SDEs, but variable definitions, coding systems and derivation rules should be consistent wherever possible.

docs.title: Data requirements for implementing the Diabetes Core Dataset
Overview
docs.text:
This page defines the input data requirements for implementing the Diabetes Core Dataset (DIA-Core) using routinely collected health data.

Implementation of DIA-Core involves two main stages:

  1. Ascertainment and classification of the diabetes cohort.
  2. Derivation of the remaining core dataset variables.

The input data requirements described below cover both stages.

The aim is to enable Secure Data Environments (SDEs) and other data providers to map their existing data structures to a common framework, identify gaps in data availability, and facilitate consistent and reproducible implementation of DIA-Core.

The tables described below represent logical data structures rather than a prescribed database schema. Data may be held across multiple tables or combined within a single table, depending on the underlying data source. Where necessary, data can be mapped to these structures using database views or intermediate tables.

The input data required will depend on the DIA-Core variables being derived and the data sources available within each SDE. Where input variables or data sources are unavailable, the implications for implementation should be documented.

docs.title: 1. Patient demographics
docs.text:
One row per patient.

Ethnicity may alternatively be derived from coded clinical observations or linked secondary care data.

docs.text:
One row per patient registration period.

Information on registration and data availability is required to establish patient observation periods and distinguish potentially incident from pre-existing diabetes diagnoses.

The data collection end date may alternatively be supplied at practice or dataset level.

docs.text:
One row per recorded clinical event or measurement.

Variable Description Format / coding system patient_id Unique patient identifier String observation_date Date of clinical event or measurement Date record_date Date on which the clinical event was recorded in the electronic health record Date clinical_code Code describing the clinical event or measurement SNOMED CT numeric_value Numeric result, where applicable Numeric unit Unit of measurement, where applicable String or coded value categorical_value Categorical result, where applicable String or coded value event_id Unique identifier for the clinical event String event_type Type or source of clinical event, where available Categorical

This includes diagnoses, clinical measurements, laboratory results, lifestyle information and other coded clinical events.

Relevant information may be stored across separate observation, problem, diagnosis and laboratory results tables. All relevant sources should be considered when deriving DIA-Core variables.

Historical records coded using Read v2 or CTV3 may also be relevant and should be mapped or processed using appropriate codelists.

docs.title: 4. Primary care medication prescriptions
docs.text:
One row per prescription record.

Variable Description Format / coding system patient_id Unique patient identifier String prescription_date Date of prescription Date medication_code Code identifying the prescribed medication or device dm+d or BNF quantity Quantity prescribed Numeric quantity_unit Unit of prescribed quantity String or coded value dose Prescribed dose or dosage instructions Numeric or string prescription_id Unique prescription identifier String

Medication records are used both for identifying and classifying individuals with diabetes and for deriving longitudinal treatment histories.

Relevant prescriptions include glucose-lowering medications, blood pressure lowering medications, lipid lowering medications, antiplatelet therapy and continuous glucose monitoring devices.

Medication codes may be provided in either dm+d or BNF format, with dm+d preferred where available. Only one coding system is required. Where necessary, codes can be mapped between coding systems using the NHS Business Services Authority BNF-SNOMED mapping dataset, although mappings are not always one-to-one.

Some SDEs may also have access to medication dispensing data in addition to prescription records. Dispensing data are used in some phenotyping algorithms, including those developed through the BHF Data Science Centre Heart Failure Phenotype Benchmarking project. Where available, relevant variables include patient identifier, dispensing date or processing period, and medication codes.

docs.title: 5. Linked secondary care data
docs.text: Linked secondary care data can supplement primary care records, particularly for identifying diabetes complications and acute clinical events.

docs.title: Hospital admissions and episodes
docs.text:
One row per hospital episode, with information enabling episodes to be grouped into admissions or continuous inpatient spells.

docs.title: Hospital diagnoses
docs.text:
One row per recorded diagnosis per episode.

Variable Description Format / coding system episode_id Unique hospital episode identifier String diagnosis_code Hospital diagnosis code ICD-10 diagnosis_position Position of diagnosis within episode Integer

All available diagnostic code positions should be retained to support implementation of the SCORE-CVD phenotyping algorithms.

docs.title: Hospital procedures
docs.text:
One row per recorded procedure per episode.

Variable Description Format / coding system episode_id Unique hospital episode identifier String procedure_code Hospital procedure code OPCS-4 procedure_date Date of procedure Date procedure_position Position of procedure within episode Integer

Additional secondary care fields may be required to implement specific cardiovascular and other phenotyping algorithms.

docs.title: 6. Linked mortality data
docs.text:
One row per deceased patient, with information on underlying and contributory causes of death. Contributory causes may alternatively be held in a separate table with multiple rows per patient.

Variable Description Format / coding system patient_id Unique patient identifier String date_of_death Date of death Date underlying_cause_of_death Underlying cause of death ICD-10 contributory_cause_of_death Other recorded causes of death ICD-10

All available contributory causes of death and their recorded positions should be retained where possible.

Where available, national mortality registration data should be used preferentially to ascertain dates and causes of death.

docs.title: 7. Input data requirements for diabetes cohort ascertainment
docs.text:
We recommend following the diabetes cohort ascertainment algorithm developed by the BHF HDR UK Diabetes Data Science Catalyst (DDSC) Defining Diabetes project.

The following data are required to implement the full primary care diabetes cohort ascertainment algorithm:

  • Patient demographics and registration information.
  • Coded diabetes diagnoses.
  • HbA1c measurements, including values and units.
  • Insulin prescription records.

The cohort ascertainment algorithm identifies individuals meeting at least one of the following criteria:

  • A recorded diabetes diagnostic code.
  • Two consecutive elevated HbA1c measurements (>=48 mmol/mol) within two years.
  • At least six months between the first and last recorded insulin prescriptions.

Where one or more data sources are unavailable, the algorithm may be partially implemented, but the resulting limitations in cohort ascertainment should be documented.

Further information, including codelists and algorithms for defining diabetes cases, diagnosis dates and diabetes type, is available from the HDR UK Phenotype Library and the Diabetes Core Dataset implementation guidance.

docs.title: 8. Mapping local data to DIA-Core
docs.text:
We recommend that each SDE maps its local data structures to the logical tables and variables described above before beginning implementation.

The mapping exercise should identify:

  • Local source tables and variable names.
  • Available clinical coding systems.
  • Required transformations or recoding.
  • Data coverage and historical availability.
  • Missing or unavailable variables.
  • Any adaptations required to implement DIA-Core algorithms.
  • This mapping should be extended to cover linked secondary care and mortality data where available.

docs.title: 9. General data considerations
docs.text:
• Patient identifiers should be consistent across all linked datasets.
  • Clinical and medication codes should be stored as strings to preserve identifier precision and formatting.
  • Dates should be provided at the highest resolution permitted by local information governance requirements.
  • Data coverage, including start and end dates, should be documented for each source.
  • Historical clinical records should be retained wherever available.
  • Missing information should be distinguishable from a confirmed absence of a clinical event.
  • Coding system versions and any mappings between coding systems should be documented.
  • Local adaptations to codelists, data cleaning rules and phenotyping algorithms should be documented to support reproducibility.
  • Derived clinical data should retain their longitudinal structure wherever possible.

docs.title: Stage 1: Diabetes cohort ascertainment and classification
Overview
docs.text:
The first stage of implementing the Diabetes Core Dataset (DIA-Core) involves identifying individuals with diabetes, determining their date and age at diagnosis, and classifying diabetes type.

We recommend following the algorithms developed by the BHF HDR UK Diabetes Data Science Catalyst (DDSC) Defining Diabetes project. The algorithms and associated codelists are also available via the HDR UK Phenotype Library.

The following sections provide step-by-step implementation guidance for applying these algorithms to routinely collected primary care data.

docs.title: Input data requirements
docs.text:
The following input data are required:

  • Patient demographics.
  • Primary care registration information.
  • Primary care clinical observations, including diabetes diagnostic codes and HbA1c measurements.
  • Primary care medication prescriptions, including insulin and non-insulin glucose-lowering medications.

See the standardised input data requirements for further details of the tables, variables and coding systems required.

docs.title: Prerequisites and general data cleaning
docs.text:
Before implementing the diabetes cohort ascertainment algorithm:

  • Date of birth should be available for all patients (at minimum, year of birth; month and year preferred). Patients without this information should be excluded.
  • Where the exact date of birth is unavailable, we have developed an algorithm for defining date of birth; however, its use may be restricted by data source-specific governance or regulatory requirements.
  • Sex should be available for all patients.
  • Additional data cleaning steps depend on the data source. For example, in CPRD we additionally exclude patients without valid registration dates, those aged over 115 years, and those from practices with anomalous mortality rates.
  • Date of death should preferentially be obtained from national mortality registration data over primary or secondary care recorded dates, where available.
  • Relevant historical diabetes diagnostic codes may be stored in different source tables, such as problem or observation tables.
  • The last observable date should reflect the end of available follow-up for each patient, taking into account the data collection end date, deregistration date and date of death, where applicable.

docs.title: Implementation overview
docs.text:
The implementation is divided into four components:

  1. Extraction and cleaning of diabetes-related clinical and medication records.
  2. Identification of individuals with diabetes.
  3. Derivation of diabetes diagnosis date and age at diagnosis.
  4. Classification of diabetes type.

docs.title: A. Extraction and cleaning of diabetes-related records
A1. Diabetes diagnostic codes
docs.text:
Use the diabetes diagnostic codelists to extract and clean all instances of diabetes diagnostic codes.

Step Description Output Quality assurance A1.1 Extract and clean all diabetes diagnostic codes, categorised as type 1, type 2, other or not otherwise specified (NOS). Longitudinal table containing patient identifier, observation date and diabetes code category. Distribution of code dates. Number and percentage of patients with diabetes diagnostic codes. A1.2 Identify the earliest clean diabetes diagnostic code per patient. One row per patient with earliest diabetes code date. Distribution of earliest diabetes code dates. A1.3 Count type 1 and type 2-specific diabetes codes per patient. One row per patient with counts of type 1 and type 2-specific codes. Distribution of code counts and number of patients with codes for both types.

docs.title: A2. HbA1c measurements
docs.text:
Use the HbA1c codelists and cleaning rules to identify and clean all available HbA1c measurements.

Step Description Output Quality assurance A2.1 Extract and clean all HbA1c measurements, standardising values to mmol/mol. Combine multiple measurements on the same day according to the HbA1c cleaning rules. Longitudinal table containing patient identifier, measurement date and cleaned HbA1c value. One row per patient per date. Distribution of HbA1c values and measurement dates. A2.2 Identify the earliest elevated HbA1c measurement (>=48 mmol/mol) per patient. One row per patient with earliest elevated HbA1c date. Distribution of dates and number of patients with elevated HbA1c. A2.3 Identify patients with two consecutive elevated HbA1c measurements (>=48 mmol/mol) within two years, with no intervening non-elevated measurement. Retain the date of the first measurement in the earliest qualifying pair. One row per patient meeting this criterion, including the date of the first elevated HbA1c in the qualifying pair. Number of patients meeting the criterion.

docs.title: A3. Glucose-lowering medication prescriptions
docs.text:
Use the diabetes medication codelists to extract and clean insulin and non-insulin glucose-lowering medication prescriptions.

Step Description Output Quality assurance A3.1 Extract and clean all insulin and non-insulin glucose-lowering medication prescriptions. Longitudinal prescription tables containing patient identifier, prescription date, drug class, drug substance, and available dose and quantity information. Distribution of prescription dates. Number of patients prescribed insulin, non-insulin glucose-lowering medications, and both. A3.2 Identify the earliest and latest insulin prescription dates per patient. Calculate the number of days between these dates and the number of days between the latest insulin prescription and the last observable date. One row per patient with earliest and latest insulin prescription dates, duration of recorded insulin use and time since latest prescription. Distribution of duration of recorded insulin use and time since latest insulin prescription.

There may be multiple prescriptions for an individual on the same date. These should be retained where they represent distinct prescriptions.

docs.title: B. Identification of individuals with diabetes
docs.text:
Individuals meeting at least one of the following criteria are identified as diabetes cases:

  1. A recorded diabetes diagnostic code.
  2. Two consecutive elevated HbA1c measurements (>=48 mmol/mol) within two years.
  3. At least 183 days between the earliest and latest recorded insulin prescriptions.
Step Description Output Quality assurance B1 Combine the patient-level information derived in section A to identify individuals meeting at least one of the three diabetes ascertainment criteria. One row per patient with diabetes, including separate binary indicators for each ascertainment criterion. Total number and percentage of patients identified as diabetes cases. Number of patients meeting each criterion and each combination of criteria.

Retaining separate indicators for the three criteria enables comparison of the relative contribution of different data sources to diabetes ascertainment.

docs.title: C. Derivation of diabetes diagnosis date and age
docs.text:
For individuals identified as having diabetes, use the earliest diabetes diagnostic code and elevated HbA1c measurements to estimate the date of diabetes diagnosis, following the DDSC algorithm.

Step Description Output Quality assurance C1 Derive diabetes diagnosis date using the earliest diabetes diagnostic code and the first elevated HbA1c measurement from the earliest qualifying pair, following the diabetes diagnosis date algorithm. One row per patient with estimated diabetes diagnosis date. Distribution of diagnosis dates and number of patients with missing diagnosis dates. C2 Identify diagnosis dates within -30 to +90 days (inclusive) of GP registration start date, as these may represent pre-existing diagnoses. Indicator of potentially unreliable diagnosis dates. Number and percentage of patients with diagnosis dates around registration. C3 Calculate time from diabetes diagnosis to earliest insulin prescription in days. Identify patients whose earliest insulin prescription occurred more than one year before the estimated diagnosis date. Time from diagnosis to insulin initiation and indicator of potentially unreliable diagnosis dates. Distribution of time from diagnosis to insulin initiation. C4 Apply diagnosis date cleaning rules and calculate age at diagnosis using patient date of birth, to one decimal point where date precision permits. Cleaned diabetes diagnosis date and age at diagnosis. Distribution of diagnosis dates and ages. Number and percentage of patients with missing diagnosis date or age.

We recommend setting potentially unreliable diagnosis dates to missing where they occur around GP registration or where insulin initiation predates the estimated diagnosis date by more than one year. Individuals should remain in the diabetes cohort even if their diagnosis date cannot be reliably determined.

See the diabetes diagnosis date rules for further information.

docs.title: D. Classification of diabetes type
docs.text:
Apply the DDSC diabetes classification algorithm using the diabetes diagnostic codes, diagnosis information and medication prescription history derived in the preceding steps.

Step Description Output Quality assurance D1 Apply the DDSC diabetes type classification algorithm. One row per patient with assigned diabetes classification. Number and percentage of patients in each diabetes classification category. D2 Combine diabetes classification with diabetes diagnosis date and age at diagnosis. Patient-level diabetes cohort. Distribution of age at diagnosis by diabetes type and percentage with missing diagnosis dates.

The DDSC algorithm assigns individuals to the following categories:

  • Type 1 diabetes.
  • Type 2 diabetes.
  • Diabetes other.
  • Diabetes not otherwise specified (NOS).
  • Diabetes unlikely.

See the diabetes classification rules for further information, including classification of individuals with conflicting type 1 and type 2 diabetes diagnostic codes.

Diabetes remission should be recorded separately from diabetes type, where information is available.

docs.title: Output of Stage 1
docs.text:
The output of Stage 1 is a patient-level diabetes cohort with one row per patient.

We recommend retaining the following variables to support reproducibility and quality assurance:

Variable Description patient_id Unique pseudonymous patient identifier diabetes_code Indicator of meeting the diabetes diagnostic code criterion elevated_hba1c_pair Indicator of meeting the elevated HbA1c criterion insulin_6months Indicator of meeting the insulin prescription criterion earliest_diabetes_code_date Earliest clean diabetes diagnostic code date earliest_elevated_hba1c_date Earliest elevated HbA1c measurement date earliest_qualifying_hba1c_date First measurement date in the earliest qualifying HbA1c pair earliest_insulin_date Earliest recorded insulin prescription date latest_insulin_date Latest recorded insulin prescription date diabetes_diagnosis_date Estimated diabetes diagnosis date after cleaning diabetes_diagnosis_age Estimated age at diabetes diagnosis diagnosis_near_registration Indicator of diagnosis date around GP registration insulin_before_diagnosis Indicator of insulin initiation more than one year before estimated diagnosis time_to_insulin Time from diabetes diagnosis to earliest insulin prescription type1_code_count Number of type 1-specific diabetes codes type2_code_count Number of type 2-specific diabetes codes diabetes_type Diabetes classification derived using the DDSC algorithm

Individuals classified as 'diabetes unlikely' should be retained in the intermediate output for quality assurance, with their inclusion or exclusion from the final diabetes cohort documented.

The longitudinal tables of cleaned diabetes diagnostic codes, HbA1c measurements and glucose-lowering medication prescriptions should also be retained.

The diabetes cohort can then be used to implement Stage 2: Derivation of the remaining DIA-Core variables.

docs.title: Quality assurance
docs.text:
For continuous variables and dates, we recommend reporting the minimum, 25th percentile, median, 75th percentile, maximum and mode, where appropriate.

For categorical variables, we recommend reporting counts, percentages and missingness.

Quality assurance outputs should be reviewed at each stage of the implementation to identify potential data quality issues and unexpected differences between data sources.

docs.title: Ethnicity mapping
docs.text: Ethnicity was a free-text field in the original dataset; these have been mapped to the broad and narrow 2021 UK Census categories. The lookup csv file (see bottom of this page) includes the mappings, and also a 'standardised ethnicity' column which seeks to harmonise identical ethnicities where these were originally recorded differently. The standardised ethnicity column is to be used in conjunction with categorised ethnicity as some ethnicities recorded in this column appear in multiple categories e.g. Armenian appears in both White and Asian groups and Chechnyan in the White and Other groups.

docs.title: Further detail on mapping
docs.text:
• Minor misspellings have been corrected (See 'Notes' column of lookup)
  • Some ethnicities were treated as missing if not clear
  • If a ethnicity is explicitly stated (e.g. White, Black, Asian, Arabic, Caucasian, African), this takes precedence over additional information that may indicate nationality rather than ethnicity (e.g. British, Italian)
  • Individuals were only be classified as "Mixed" if they explicitly self-identify as mixed (e.g. use the term "mixed") or if two distinct ethnicities are clearly stated. Individuals were not classified as mixed based solely on combinations that may represent nationalities rather than ethnicities.
  • Turkish is included in White ethnicity unless further information to the contrary provided
